subsection.title: Population of a City
subsection.paragraph: Suppose the plane region $$R$$ represents a certain district of a city and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives the population density (the number of people per square mile) at any point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$R$$ . Enclose the set $$R$$ by a rectangle, and construct a grid for it in the usual manner. In any rectangular region of the grid that has no point in common with $$R$$ , set $$f\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)hk = 0$$ (Figure 42). Then, corresponding to any grid covering the set $$R$$ , the general term of the Riemann sum $$f\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)hk$$ (population density times area) gives the number of people living in that part of the city corresponding to the rectangular region $$R_{i}$$ . Therefore, the Riemann sum gives an approximation of the number of people living in the district represented by $$R$$ and, in the limit, the double integral
gives the actual number of people living in the district under consideration.

subsection.title: Average Value of a Function
subsection.paragraph: In Section 6.5, we showed that the average value of a continuous function $$f(x)$$ over an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is given by

That is, the average value of a function over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is the integral of $$f$$ over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ divided by the length of the interval. An analogous result holds for a function of two variables $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over a plane region $$R$$ . To see this, we enclose $$R$$ by a rectangle and construct a rectangular grid. Let $$\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)$$ be any point in the rectangle $$R_{i}$$ of area $$hk$$ . Now, the average value of the $$mn$$ numbers $${f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)},{f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right)},\ldots,{f\left( {x_{mn},y_{mn}} \right)}$$ is given by

Suppose $$f$$ is nonnegative and continuous over the plane region $$R$$ . Then, the average value of $$f$$ over $$R$$ can be thought of as the (constant) height of the cylinder with base $$R$$ and volume that is exactly equal to the volume of the solid under the graph of $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .
